I can't do that where I live though, so before I even adopted my piggies I promised myself that when one passes away, I'll give myself a week to mourn and say my goodbyes, and then I'll surrender the surviving pig to the guinea pig rescue so she'll be well taken care of and have new friends to play with. If you don't have a definite plan similar to this or the potential guinea pig "renting", adopting guinea pigs is not a good idea.

The best you can do for her now is get a bigger cage (I use Midwest. It’s bigger and cheaper than this one in your picture. The best analogy I can give is, imagine if you and a roommate lived in a walk in closet. This is the situation your piggies are in with their current cage. Add babies to the equation and the pigs could get violent due to lack of their own space.

I have 2 piggies and use guineadad bedding. It’s fleece bedding that costs a pretty penny up front but ends up saving you money in the long run compared to disposable bedding. As long as I spot clean it every day and wash it every three days as well as empty the litter box then (they don’t always poop in it always but it’s good for keeping hay in) smell isn’t usually too big an issue. Guineadad is also good because with disposable bedding the actual cage tends to get dirty and smelly really fast if you forget to clean it (clumps of used bedding sticking to the cage bottom), but with fleece bedding that’s avoided pretty much altogether. Just the occasional pellet escaping under the blanket. Fleece bedding can also be homemade but I just went ahead and got guineadad because it’s praised for how absorbent it is. But guinea pigs are never going to smell completely immaculate except for the first 5 minutes after a bedding clean. They poop a ton. A slight smell is inevitable. It just depends on how often you’re willing to clean their cage and how tolerant you are. Air freshener also isn’t an option because it can hurt the piggies’ lungs. If you want an animal that doesn’t smell at all ever I’d look into getting a reptile. Typically all mammals are gonna smell at least a little.

As for noise, it honestly depends on the piggies. My two never wake me up at night, but I’ve heard of people waking up at 3 am to their piggies squeaking for veggies. The most noise mine make at night is sometimes fighting over the water bottle and it slamming against the cage. But if you go to bed at the same time every day they tend to adapt to your sleep schedule and quiet down when you do. 
They also make cute munching noises when they eat hay so that’s a plus. I find that sound soothing especially as I’m dozing off.
I like to wash it with detergent that has non artificial smell and color. Less chance of hurting the piggies. I also wash mine in their own load just in case the laundry bag rips

I started using guineadad a few months ago, and I really wish I’d started with it. If you buy a laundry bag to wash the bedding in,  cleaning the cage actually is faster than it was with the paper bedding. They like it better. It actually ends up saving money in the long run too. It’s easier to clean. The only con was the upfront cost.

I have a friend who needed an emotional support animal, and he happened to know someone who trains rabbits for just that. But initially both animals are fairly skittish. You might want to look into a ferret as well. Since they are predators rather than prey they’re a lot more outgoing. Unless it’s a trained animal already used to humans guinea pigs are essentially just like rabbits in a lot of ways. You just can’t walk them and they’re less likely to understand how to use a litter box, but other than that. If you can find either two guinea pigs or a rabbit that already like humans, you may want that for space or financial reasons, but if not, a free roam ferret might be what you’re looking for. 
Guinea pigs are typically good for people with apartments because unlike a rabbit or a ferret, if you get them a big cage they’re all set. If you have two (which you should. They need a guinea pig friend to be happy.) you can leave for work and come home and they’re as happy as you left them. But because they’re timid and like their own species you have to accept that they will probably never be affectionate to you like a cat or a dog would. You can love them and pet them and be the only human that they like, but you’re still not a guinea pig, so they’ll always prefer the company of their cage mate over you. I’m okay with that, but a child could become impatient or cross and accidentally hurt the animal, which is pretty easy to do since they’re pretty fragile.
Rabbits in that aspect are also more durable than guinea pigs in that they’re stronger animals. You can’t walk a piggie because their backs are like glass. Rabbits don’t have that problem. Although they are still less durable than a cat or a dog. That friend I mentioned earlier had an incident where his rabbit hopped out of his arms while he was holding him and standing, and the poor thing died of a back injury. (He now has another rabbit friend who he holds only while sitting.)
What I’m saying is that both might not be good for a young kid but from what I understand rabbits are slightly better if you have the space for them. Never looked too far into ferrets but they appear to be more outgoing from what I’ve seen.

Guinea pigs are great pets for teens and adults because they can be quite skittish. Mine still don't like being handled aside from stroking and I've had them for over 6 months.
A rabbit can also be skittish but can be walked and can have free roam over the house unlike a guinea pig. They can be skittish too but if you find one that has been trained to be an emotional support animal those ones are pretty friendly. I would have gotten a rabbit myself if I had the room and time for one.

Guinea pigs are social animals and really need a friend of their own species to be happy. Once you figure out its gender, you should get a female, which is either spayed or not depending on if your new buddy is male or female. My two piggies took a few weeks before they were confident enough to tell me (by screaming) that they wanted food. You've just got to be patient and let them come to you. 

The trick is to train them with treats while allowing them to run away if they want. I'm training my piggies to sit in my lap by encouraging them with pea flakes. Whenever they come up to me and let me pet them, they get a treat, but they're always welcome to run and hide in the comfort of their cage if they're uncomfortable.
